items.stem: A student argues that societies without writing were 'not yet civilised'. Why do historians reject this framing?

options.text: 'Civilisation' describes forms of social complexity, not a moral rank, and oral societies were complex in other ways
options.rationale: Correct: the term is descriptive, and writing is one feature among many, not a universal threshold of worth.

options.text: Because all societies eventually developed writing
options.rationale: Many societies remained non-literate; the point is the ranking itself is flawed.

options.text: Because writing was invented only once
options.rationale: Writing arose independently in several regions; this does not address the value judgement.

options.text: Because civilisation requires cities, which all societies had
options.rationale: Not all societies were urban; the error is treating complexity as a single ladder.

items.explanation: Correct: the term is descriptive, and writing is one feature among many, not a universal threshold of worth.

items.stem: Which TWO developments most directly connected distant societies across Afro-Eurasia before 1500? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Long-distance trade networks such as the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean routes
options.rationale: Correct: these routes moved goods, people and ideas between regions.

options.text: The spread of universalising religions along those routes
options.rationale: Correct: faiths like Buddhism and Islam travelled with merchants and migrants.
That belongs to the post-1500 Atlantic world.

items.stem: Why do historians treat the boundary between 'medieval' and 'early modern' as an interpretation rather than a fixed date?

options.text: Periodisation is a tool for analysis; change was gradual and uneven across regions
options.rationale: Correct: labels are imposed by historians to organise continuous change, and fit regions differently.

options.text: Because no sources survive from the transition
options.rationale: Abundant sources survive; the issue is interpretive framing.

options.text: Because the calendar changed at that point everywhere
options.rationale: Calendar reforms were local and are not the basis of the division.

options.text: Because all historians agree on the exact year
options.rationale: They do not agree, which is precisely why it is interpretive.

items.explanation: Correct: labels are imposed by historians to organise continuous change, and fit regions differently.
